title: If Mithila burns
hookLine: a king hears his city is on fire and says nothing of his burns
carry: asakta: do the work, don't be owned by it
tomorrow: a king asks every monk: who is greater, the monk or the householder?
last: EVERY ACT CAN BE AN OFFERING.

lines: A KING WHO KNEW THE SELF.
cards: In that same talk, Krishna gives Arjuna an example: King Janaka, who reached perfection through action. Janaka ruled Mithila, with courts to run and people to feed, and sages honored him as a king who knew the self.
The Mahabharata keeps a short song of his, and storytellers love to stage it. A messenger runs into the hall shouting that the city is on fire. Everyone leaps up.
Janaka says: my wealth is endless, because nothing is mine. If Mithila burns, nothing of mine burns.

teach.b: Hear it the wrong way and it sounds cold: the city burns and the king shrugs. But Krishna points to Janaka for the opposite reason.

teach.h: ACT FOR THE GOOD OF THE WORLD.
teach.b: Janaka and others like him reached perfection through action, he says, and then he tells Arjuna: you too should act for lokasangraha, the holding together of the world, the good of everyone.
Janaka ran the kingdom, all of it. What he didn't do was belong to any of it. The kingdom was his work, not his self.
Krishna's word for this is asakta, unattached. So, he tells Arjuna, unattached, always do the work that's yours to do. That's karma yoga's other half.
Yesterday: offer the act. Today: stop owning it, and its results.
Swami Vivekananda, a Hindu monk who gave talks in New York in the 1890s, later printed as Karma-Yoga, put it in words his listeners could carry to the office: work like a master, not a slave.
The slave works for the wage and the praise, and is miserable when they don't come. The master gives the work everything, and is free either way.

Many teachers say it's what lets a person care well: a doctor who isn't owned by her pride can admit a mistake; a parent who isn't owned by the report card can still love the child who brought it home.
And under it all is the Gita's teaching from chapter two: you are the atman, the self, which no weapon cuts and no fire burns.

teach.h: DO THE WORK. DON'T BE OWNED BY IT.
teach.b: The city was never what Janaka was. Many teachers say that's how he could rule it so well.

how: Janaka is remembered in Hindu tradition as the rajarshi, the king-sage who ruled fully without clinging; many Hindus end a task by offering its results to God, and Vivekananda's Karma-Yoga is still read in Vedanta societies.

o: uninterested: not caring how the work turns out
unattached: working fully without clinging to results
unmoving: refusing to act so nothing can bind you

games.q: the king who owned nothing — tap the pairs.
p: the good of the whole world
gives the work everything, free either way

s: for Krishna, being unattached means not caring how things turn out
he points to Janaka, who reached perfection through action, and asks Arjuna to act for the good of the world.
Krishna names King Janaka as someone who reached perfection through action
in the same talk where Arjuna wants to quit.
Vivekananda told his New York listeners to quit their jobs
he taught them to work like a master, not a slave.

games.q: a messenger runs in: the city is on fire! by karma yoga, which king gets it right?
o: the one who panics: everything he owns is burning.
the one who shrugs: none of it is his, so why bother.
the one who sends help at once, calmly: the people are his duty, not his possessions.
games.why: unattached isn't uncaring. Krishna holds up Janaka, who reached perfection through action, and asks Arjuna to act for the good of the world while owning none of it.

practice: Think of a piece of work you're worried about, how it'll land, who'll notice. Now separate the two, the way Janaka did: the work, which is yours to do well and for others' good, and the result, which was never yours to own.
Give the work your care; set the result down. If you pray, hand the result to God, as many Hindus do, with a quiet Krishnarpanam; if not, say quietly: done, and the rest isn't mine.

wordCard.voice: Asakta, unattached. Krishna: unattached, always do the work that's yours. Janaka ruled a whole kingdom that way.

orig.note: Sanskrit: asakta, unattached; Krishna asks Arjuna to do his work asakta, without attachment (Gita 3.19).

carryVoice: Your line: asakta: do the work, don't be owned by it. If Mithila burns, nothing of mine burns. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 3.19–20 (work unattached; Janaka and others reached perfection through action; act with lokasangraha, the good of the world, in view)
Bhagavad Gita 2.23 (weapons do not cut the self, fire does not burn it)
Mahabharata, Shanti Parva (Janaka's verse: if Mithila burns, nothing of mine burns)
Swami Vivekananda, Karma-Yoga (1896), ch. 3 (the secret of work: work like a master, not a slave)
